entry.title: Hacktoberfest 2026: 28 first-time contributors, 46 merged pull requests 🦔
entry.summary: The Img2Num Hacktoberfest 2026 recap: what 28 first-time contributors shipped in 46 merged pull requests across the C++ core, the GPU path, the Python and JavaScript packages, the example apps, the docs and CI - and where to collect your badge.
entry.content:
At the end of September we asked you to contribute to Img2Num this Hacktoberfest, and we were upfront about the deal: Hacktoberfest 2026 stopped counting pull requests, so there was no counter to climb and no t-shirt at the end of it. A reviewed and merged pull request in a real project was the whole prize and

twenty-eight of you took it!

Between 3 and 30 October we merged 46 pull requests from 28 contributors. None of the contributors had contributed to Img2Num before October. They fixed output bugs in the C++ core, made the Python bindings release the GIL, gave the npm package TypeScript types, rebuilt pages of this site, and deleted more than 1 300 lines of code that was no longer needed. Every one of them is now listed on the Hacktoberfest 2026 event page, along with their pull requests.

This post is the long version that explains what got built, what it changed, and what happens next.

The numbers​

  • 28 contributors, every one of them merging into Img2Num for the first time. GitHub's contributor graph for October has the same names.
  • 46 pull requests merged between 3 and 30 October (the full list on GitHub). Maintainers' own pull requests (five, including the new CLI) are not counted.
  • 177 files changed, +5 232, and −2 959 lines.
  • At least 29 issues closed by those pull requests.
  • Under four days from opening a pull request to merging it, at the median. Twelve merged within a day; 37 of the 46 within a week.
  • 10 contributors opened more than one pull request. Three of them, @Lothnic, @saptadeep12, and @nitin-kumar-code opened five each.

What got built​

This section groups the changes according to where they were made in the project. Pull request numbers link to GitHub, and the event page has the same work grouped by person.

C++ core and GPU (8)​

  • A reusable WebGPU helper layer - #658 by @siddharth1407. RAII wrappers over Dawn (gpu::Buffer<T>, gpu::Texture, bind-group and compute-pass helpers), then both GPU kernels ported onto them: the bilateral filter went from 313 lines to 120 with identical behaviour. #694 documented the new layer the same week.
  • Two more ways to fall back to the CPU - #663 by @ayusharora07 stops the WebGPU device being initialised twice and falls back when device creation fails; #696 by @BhoomiMahna does the same when the only adapter Dawn can find is the Null backend. A machine without a usable GPU now gets the CPU path instead of a failed conversion.
  • Correct output at the edges - #659 by @RahulKumarBaldia. gaussian_blur_fft now uses reflect padding, which fixes darkened borders and content wrapping around from the opposite edge.
  • k-means with k = 1 - #682 by @nitin-kumar-code fixed the CPU path's output when there is only one cluster. A two-line change; wrong output before, right output after.
  • Fewer run-to-run differences - #765 by @saptadeep12 orders each graph node's neighbours by id, so the contour graph no longer depends on the order they happened to be inserted in.
  • ptr became image - #749 by @MiyaMango renamed the parameter across the C++ core, the C ABI and the JavaScript glue. Small, and the API reference reads better now!
  • 157 lines of unreachable contour-tracing code removed - #768 by @shivangmathur2008-stack, with the matching internal docs.

Most of this shipped in cpp 0.3.0 and bindings-c 0.2.1 on 23 October.

Python (6)​

  • The GIL is released while the C++ core runs - #777 by @Lothnic. Python threads that call Img2Num now run the native work in parallel instead of taking turns, and the console example gained a two-worker ThreadPoolExecutor demo to prove it. Krasner's #784 built on it a week later to make the GPU path parallel too.
  • img2num.__version__ - #758, and Python 3.13 declared in the package classifiers - #754, both by @Lothnic.
  • Typos in config are errors now - #766 by @IvanGiovany: an unknown key in ImageToSvgConfig raises TypeError.
  • A one-line fix for a double move - #665 by @Gracy769 removed a std::move that moved the SVG string twice in labels_to_svg.
  • Wheels carry only the Python component - #767 by @Farhan-Alam-Jamal scoped the CMake install to the python component, so wheels stop picking up files that belong to other parts of the build.

None of this is on PyPI yet - the current release is 0.3.1. It ships with the next Python release, together with the new img2num command-line tool that Krasner built in #703 and @Adithya6721 documented in #801.

JavaScript and C (2)​

  • TypeScript declarations for the npm package - #670 by @saptadeep12. The declarations are generated from tightened JSDoc with tsc --allowJs --declaration, so the JSDoc stays the single source of truth; types comes first in every exports branch; and a strict-mode tsc --noEmit type test runs in CI so they cannot drift. Ships in the next npm release.
  • The C error API got real prototypes - #764 by @Ayushrawatcy009. In C, img2num_get_last_error() declares a function taking unspecified arguments; img2num_get_last_error(void) is a prototype. Shipped in bindings-c 0.2.1.

Example apps (7)​

  • The React example's Vitest suite runs again - #713 by @Lothnic. It also lost 1,370 lines of About and credits pages that had nothing to do with the library - #789 by @mrunalC27; its /credits redirect now points at the Hall of Fame - #793 by @slopgobblercobbler; and it has a README - #660 by @PrathamRanka.
  • The console apps: the Python one validates its image input - #661 by @PrathamRanka; the C++ one was tidied up - #687 by @saptadeep12; and the Node ones (ESM and CJS) have a correct usage message and an output-path option - #677 by @Astrolyte.

Docs and this website (15)​

  • The Hall of Fame - #679 by @08abhinav. The page that honours contributors was itself built by a first-time contributor: a data file of featured members, GitHub profile and merged-PR data fetched at build time, bot filtering, and fallbacks so an API hiccup cannot break the build. The events pages sit on top of it.
  • The Showcase - #644 by @dr-nullptr turned the example-apps index into /showcase, with a "Built with Img2Num" section for third-party projects and a submission page that opens a prefilled Discussion.
  • The FAQ redesigned with accordions - #623 by @flodrick; Core Concepts became a glossary - #646 by @FathimaManal; Discord in the navbar, footer and contributing guide - #689 by @saptadeep12; site styles and the navbar blur fixed - #680 by @thilakshan2003; "Edit this page" links point at dev - #770 by @satyaharendrarushidayaka-sudo.
  • Docs that match the code: min_thickness defaults documented - #655 by @Yipjunwei; black_threshold_image described as the per-channel brightness cutoff it is, in the C++ header, the Python docstring and the docs - #692 by @Lothnic; the gpu_utils layer documented - #694 by @siddharth1407; the Debug Logging guide rewritten to match the actual code - #771 by @Ayushrawatcy009; the swapped C and JavaScript rows in the API bindings tables - #762 by @mayanksingh-7974; the synchronous-API migration guidance in our own blog post corrected - #760 by @jazayush; what happens when several people claim one issue, in the contributing guide - #795 by @saptadeep12; and the new CLI guide - #801 by @Adithya6721.

Build, CI and tooling (8)​

  • CMake pinned in .versions/cmake.json, with the minimum version derived from it - #666 by @Farhan-Alam-Jamal.
  • A Docker build command in the dev script - #669 by @thisisparth187.
  • The justfile split into modules - #695 by @mrunalC27, with the console binary paths corrected afterwards - #750 by @Yipjunwei.
  • Stray dependencies removed from the root and dev-scripts packages - #759, and validate-scripts handling an optional _meta.ignore - #774, both by @mayanksingh-7974.
  • CI cancels superseded runs when you push again to an open pull request - #757 by @nitin-kumar-code.
  • 111 lines of dead release workflow removed - #799 by @mrunalC27.

The badge​

If your name is on the event page, this is yours. It comes as SVG and PNG in light and dark versions, with ready-made Markdown and HTML snippets for a README or a profile, and a credential URL you can paste into LinkedIn's Licenses & certifications. Everything is at the top of the event page.

Hacktoberfest did not count pull requests toward rewards this year. We thought 28 first merged pull requests deserved something you can keep.

How it went from our side​

A few things we noticed reviewing 46 pull requests in a month:

  • The first three days set the pace. Fourteen pull requests were opened on 1–3 October, on top of three that had been waiting since the last days of September. By 11 October, 20 had merged.
  • Small and specific merged fastest. Twelve pull requests merged within a day of being opened, and each of them did one clearly described thing. A good title and a Fixes #... line are most of the work of getting reviewed quickly.
  • Big changes landed too. The GIL release, the TypeScript declarations and the WebGPU helper layer were each several hundred lines, and all three changed what the library can do. This was not a month of typo fixes.
  • Deleting is contributing. More than a third of the changed lines were deletions. The biggest pull request of the month by lines, #789, removed 1,370 of them.
  • People stayed. Ten of the 28 opened more than one pull request.

Thanks to Krasner, who reviewed and co-authored several of these and shipped the CLI (#703) and truly parallel GPU execution (#784) in between, and to Prachi, who wrote the post that started it and posted about it on LinkedIn.

What's next​

  • Releases. cpp 0.3.0 and bindings-c 0.2.1 are out with the core and C work. The Python and JavaScript work above - the GIL release, __version__, the TypeError, Python 3.13, the TypeScript declarations and the CLI - ships in the next PyPI and npm releases.
  • The October cohort is not done. @BhoomiMahna's #702, adding C++ and C ABI test coverage, merged on 4 November - the first post-Hacktoberfest pull request from someone who started in October. We hope for far more!
  • Discord. Contributors get the Contributor role and the private channel. Post your GitHub username in Discord and we will match it to the list.
  • You do not have to wait for next October. The good first issues are still there, and so are we.

Thank you, all 28 of you. 🦔

entry.title: Contribute to Img2Num this October 🦔
entry.summary: It's [Hacktoberfest](https://hacktoberfest.com/) season! Here's how to make your first (or next) open source contribution to Img2Num, and where to start.
entry.content:
October is Hacktoberfest season, and we'd love for this to be the month you contribute to Img2Num!

Whether you're a seasoned open source contributor or someone making their very first pull request, we'd love to have you join us.

What is Hacktoberfest?​

Summary

Hacktoberfest is a month-long celebration of open source software that runs every October. It started in 2014 as a pull-request challenge, and for over a decade it introduced thousands of developers to open source.

This year is a bit different. Hacktoberfest 2026, run by Major League Hacking (MLH) and DEV with DigitalOcean, has moved away from counting pull requests and toward in-person and online events focused on building with open source AI. The reason is one every maintainer will recognise:

low-effort, AI-generated PRs were flooding projects with noise

So to be clear: contributions to Img2Num won't count toward anything official this year. No PR counter, no t-shirt. But October is still a great month to start contributing to open source, and we're still here to help you do it.

We agree with the spirit of the change, too. One well-thought-out and meaningful contribution is worth far more than ten low-effort AI-generated ones.

Where Img2Num fits in​

This year's Hacktoberfest theme is AI belongs to everyone. Img2Num isn't an LLM or agent project, but it lives in the same world: it's built on classical computer vision and machine learning, including k-means clustering for colour quantization, plus contour tracing and skeletonization.

If you're curious about how machines actually make sense of images, before any neural network gets involved, this is a great place to learn.

Why contribute to Img2Num?​

Img2Num is a fast, accurate raster-to-SVG vectorization library built in C++ with library support for C++, C, Python, and JavaScript. It is actively used, actively maintained, and actively growing - all thanks to our users and contributors.

Here's what makes contributing to Img2Num worthwhile for you:

Real experience

You'll work with C and C++, JavaScript and WebAssembly, Python, React, and Docusaurus. These are technologies used in production systems.

CV/resume material

Open source contributions are one of the best ways to demonstrate your skills to future employers. A merged PR in a real project is worth more than most personal projects.

Mentorship

We actively mentor newcomers. You will not be left alone to figure things out. We review PRs carefully and explain our feedback.

If you get stuck along the way, give us a shout on Discord - someone's usually around.

Long-term community

October is just the start. Some of our maintainers started with a single small PR.

And here's what your contributions give us:

  • More work done. The project moves faster with more hands - there's always something that needs to be done.
  • Fresh perspectives. Newcomers often spot things that long-time contributors overlook.
  • Long-term contributors. Some of the best team members started as first-timers.

New to open source? We've got you covered.​

First of all: THANK YOU!

Even the smallest contributions can be enormously helpful and the fact that you're considering contributing to an open source project is amazing.

If this is your first time exploring open source, you might be wondering where to even begin.

We know exactly how difficult and confusing it can feel when you start contributing to open source. There are unfamiliar repositories, contribution guidelines, issues, pull requests, branches, reviews, and a lot of new terminology to figure out. Your first contribution can feel much more complicated than it actually is.

That's why we've created a bunch of Good First Issues specifically for newcomers. You don't need to be an open source expert to get started, and you don't need to know everything before making your first contribution.

Good First Issues

Find small bugs, documentation updates, and isolated features curated for new contributors.

View Issues on GitHub →

Start with an issue that interests you, read the contributing guide, and ask questions whenever you're stuck. We'll help you understand the project and the contribution process along the way.

And don't worry if your first contribution is something small. Fixing documentation, improving an example, adding a test, fixing a typo, or making a small improvement is still a real contribution that we need!

If you're new to open source, we've got you covered. 🦔

Check out our Good First Issues and find something that feels approachable.

Beyond Img2Num​

While you're in the open source spirit, we'd also encourage you to look beyond Img2Num.

Img2Num is built on top of and alongside several amazing open source projects. These projects provide important building blocks and baseline functionality that help make Img2Num possible.

If you enjoy working on Img2Num, you might also find something interesting to contribute to in the projects we depend on:

  • Dawn. Google's WebGPU implementation, which powers our GPU acceleration.
  • spdlog. The fast C++ logging library we use.
  • STB. Single-file C libraries used in our example apps.
  • Pybind11. The library that allows us to make our Python library possible.
  • Emscripten. The compiler toolchain that converts our C++ code into WebAssembly, which powers our JavaScript library.
  • Docusaurus. The framework that powers our documentation site.
  • OpenCV. Used in our Python example app.

These projects are a small part of the open source ecosystem that Img2Num is built with and around. They have their own issues, documentation, tests, features, and communities that can benefit from new contributors too.

There are many more open source projects that have made Img2Num possible. If you contribute towards improving one of them, you're basically improving Img2Num.

So if you find yourself thinking, "I want to contribute to open source, but maybe Img2Num isn't the right project for me," that's completely fine.

Explore these projects, find something that interests you, and make your first contribution there.

Every contribution to any open source project makes the ecosystem better for everyone.

See you in October 🦔​

We're excited to meet you. Whether you fix a typo or implement a feature, your contribution matters.

Come say hello on our Discord server for quick questions and chat, or open a thread in our Discussions for ideas, proposals, and anything worth keeping searchable. Then pick up an issue, and let's build something great together.

entry.title: Img2Num JS 0.4.2: One npm Package, Five Purpose-Built WebAssembly Bundles
entry.summary: Img2Num 0.4.2 ships five purpose-built WASM bundles on npm - browser ESM, IIFE, UMD, and Node ESM/CJS - fixing CommonJS require() crashes and bundler .wasm resolution for image-to-SVG conversion in JavaScript.
entry.content:
Img2Num's JavaScript package v0.4.2 is out on npm, and it's the biggest change to the npm distribution since we first shipped WebAssembly builds.

In short, instead of one compromise bundle, the package now ships five purpose-built bundles, each backed by its own Emscripten glue variant, and getting started no longer requires knowing anything about Emscripten - regardless of whether you're in a bundled web app, a plain <script> tag, or Node.js.

If you're new here: Img2Num is a C++-based library for converting raster images into clean SVGs, with bindings for C, Python, and JavaScript. This release is about the JavaScript and WebAssembly side of the library - the C++ core, C API, and Python package are unchanged.

Why 0.4.2 and not 0.4.0?

Because our example apps kept catching bugs faster than we could write this post.

0.4.0 shipped everything described below - plus two latent bugs, one per environment. In the browser, the published wasm URL wasn't statically detectable by bundlers, so bundled apps (Vite, webpack, Rollup) hit a 404 on img2num.wasm at runtime. Our own React example caught it the same day, and 0.4.0 is now deprecated on npm.

0.4.1 fixed the browser build - but CommonJS was still broken. require("img2num") crashed on Node < 22.12 with ERR_REQUIRE_ESM instead of converting: our load of the ESM-only webgpu package was compiled into a top-level require() call, and when that failed, the promised CPU fallback died too - the Emscripten glue dereferences navigator, which doesn't exist in Node, so the conversion aborted with navigator is not defined instead of falling back. Node >= 22.12 supports require() of ES modules and masked all of this, which is exactly why our dev machines never saw it. Our new Node CJS example caught it two days later.

0.4.2 is the release as intended, and it exists specifically to make CommonJS work: the webgpu load is now a real dynamic import() in the CJS output, and the fallback path installs a stub navigator.gpu so the glue genuinely routes to the CPU. Both bug classes now have build-time guards that inspect the emitted bundles and fail the build if either regression ever reappears - because both times, the source was correct and the published artifact wasn't.

Why we rebuilt the build​

Until now, the npm package shipped a single Emscripten build that tried to work everywhere. It mostly did - but "mostly" meant subtle path-resolution bugs when bundlers relocated the .wasm file, awkward CJS/ESM interop in Node, and a <script>-tag story that was harder than it should have been (it was basically unusable).

The underlying problem is that one Emscripten glue cannot serve every consumption mode. ES6-style glue emits top-level await and import.meta, which UMD and IIFE chunks can't carry. CJS-shaped glue reads __dirname, which ESM doesn't have. Web glue drags XHR branches into Node; Node glue drags fs/path branches into the browser. No single artifact can be all of these at once, so we stopped trying to make that idea work.

0.4.2 builds three WASM variants (web, standalone (iife/umd), node) through a parameterized CMake function, then emits five bundles from per-target Vite configs:

BundleFormatWASMUse case
dist/browser/img2num.jsESMExternal .wasmBundled web apps (Vite, webpack, Rollup)
dist/standalone/img2num.iife.jsIIFEInlinedPlain <script> tag, CDNs
dist/standalone/img2num.umd.jsUMDInlinedAMD/RequireJS and legacy loaders
dist/node/img2num.jsESMExternal .wasmModern Node projects (import)
dist/node/img2num.cjsCJSExternal .wasmExisting CommonJS codebases (require())

Your package manager and bundler pick the right one automatically via the exports map - you just import { ... } from "img2num" (or require it) and it'll work.

The WASM strategy differs by target on purpose. The standalone IIFE/UMD builds inline the binary, so a <script> tag loads one file with no path resolution at all. The browser ESM and Node builds ship a real sibling .wasm file that your bundler resolves and copies via new URL(..., import.meta.url) - we had to actively defeat Vite's lib-mode habit of inlining it as a data URL, which cut the browser entry from ~900 kB to ~108 kB. That tug-of-war is exactly what bit 0.4.0: our anti-inlining trick also hid the URL from your bundler. 0.4.1 fixed it by mangling the URL only during our build and restoring the bundler-detectable literal in the published output, so both sides of the fight now win - and a build guard fails loudly if the literal ever goes missing again.

The Node builds fight a different interop battle - the one that forced 0.4.2. The optional GPU path loads the webgpu package, which is ESM-only - so the CJS bundle has to load it with a dynamic import(), the one form of ESM loading that works inside CommonJS everywhere. 0.4.0 and 0.4.1 shipped that as a compiled-in require() (see the warning above); 0.4.2 ships the real import(), and if webgpu is missing or fails to load for any reason, Img2Num now installs a stub navigator.gpu so the WASM glue genuinely falls back to the CPU instead of crashing on navigator is not defined. A matching build guard scans the emitted CJS chunk and fails the build if any executable require("webgpu") ever sneaks back in.

How to use Img2Num in the browser and Node.js​

The same two calls - decode to pixels, convert to SVG - work in every environment. Here's the shortest working version of each target, with a live sandbox to poke at:

  • Browser ESM
  • IIFE
  • UMD (RequireJS)
  • Node ESM
  • Node CJS

For bundled apps (Vite, webpack, Rollup) or a native <script type="module"> - the exports map resolves the browser build automatically:

import { imageToUint8ClampedArray, imageToSvg } from "img2num";

const fileInput = document.querySelector("#fileInput");

fileInput.addEventListener("change", async (e) => {
  const { pixels, width, height } = await imageToUint8ClampedArray(e.target.files[0]);
  const { svg } = await imageToSvg({ pixels, width, height });

  document.querySelector("#preview").src = "data:image/svg+xml;base64," + btoa(svg);
});

Try it on CodeSandbox

One plain <script> tag, one global Img2Num object - the WASM is inlined, so there's nothing else to serve:

<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/img2num@0.4.2/dist/standalone/img2num.iife.js"></script>
<script>
  const { imageToUint8ClampedArray, imageToSvg } = Img2Num;

  fileInput.addEventListener("change", async (e) => {
    const { pixels, width, height } = await imageToUint8ClampedArray(e.target.files[0]);
    const { svg } = await imageToSvg({ pixels, width, height });
    preview.src = "data:image/svg+xml;base64," + btoa(svg);
  });
</script>

Try it on CodeSandbox

Loaded as an AMD module - nothing is added to the global scope:

<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/requirejs@2.3.8/require.js"></script>
<script>
  requirejs.config({
    paths: { img2num: "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/img2num@0.4.2/dist/standalone/img2num.umd" },
  });

  requirejs(["img2num"], ({ imageToUint8ClampedArray, imageToSvg }) => {
    fileInput.addEventListener("change", async (e) => {
      const { pixels, width, height } = await imageToUint8ClampedArray(e.target.files[0]);
      const { svg } = await imageToSvg({ pixels, width, height });
      preview.src = "data:image/svg+xml;base64," + btoa(svg);
    });
  });
</script>

Try it on CodeSandbox

import resolves the Node ESM build. Decode with whatever you like - here, sharp:

import { writeFileSync } from "fs";
import { imageToSvg, terminateWasmModule } from "img2num";
import sharp from "sharp";

const { data, info } = await sharp("input.png").ensureAlpha().raw().toBuffer({ resolveWithObject: true });

const pixels = new Uint8ClampedArray(data.buffer, data.byteOffset, data.byteLength);

try {
  const { svg } = await imageToSvg({ pixels, width: info.width, height: info.height });
  writeFileSync("output.svg", svg);
} finally {
  await terminateWasmModule();
}

Try it on CodeSandbox

require() resolves the CJS build - the one this release exists to fix. No flags, no interop wrappers:

const { writeFileSync } = require("fs");
const { imageToSvg, terminateWasmModule } = require("img2num");
const sharp = require("sharp");

async function main() {
  const { data, info } = await sharp("input.png").ensureAlpha().raw().toBuffer({ resolveWithObject: true });

  const pixels = new Uint8ClampedArray(data.buffer, data.byteOffset, data.byteLength);

  try {
    const { svg } = await imageToSvg({ pixels, width: info.width, height: info.height });
    writeFileSync("output.svg", svg);
  } finally {
    await terminateWasmModule();
  }
}

main().catch(console.error);

Try it on CodeSandbox

Breaking changes​

This is a majorish release for a reason, though migration is small for most codebases:

dist/ layout and filenames have changed.
  • If you were deep-importing into dist/, update those paths to the table above.
  • If you import the package root, you don't have to change anything.
Export conditions are reordered.

The browser condition now comes first, so bundlers targeting the browser actually get the browser build - previously they matched import first and silently received the Node build. If your bundle got smaller and your weird workaround stopped being necessary, that's why.

Minimum supported Node is now v18.

Previously we documented Node >= 14; the new node-glue builds require version 18.

Other Improvements

Two quieter improvements ride along:

  1. The optional webgpu dependency in Node is now properly guarded: if it's missing (--ignore-optional), fails to install on your platform, or can't be loaded, Img2Num logs a warning and falls back to CPU instead of throwing. (0.4.0 and 0.4.1 claimed this and didn't deliver it - the fallback path itself crashed. 0.4.2 delivers it, verified against both the ESM and CJS console examples with webgpu removed.)

  2. Initial WASM memory dropped from 2 GB to 32 MB - a 2 GB reservation fails outright on mobile Safari and bought nothing with memory growth enabled.

What happened to the Web Worker?​

That was last release. 0.3.0 removed the internal Web Worker, so every call now runs on the thread that makes it - Img2Num does the math, you decide where it runs. The functions are still async, though, so keep your await: without it you get a Promise back instead of a result. If you're moving from an earlier version straight to v0.4.2, the 0.3.0 migration still applies: if you need to keep the main thread free, wrap calls in your own worker:

// worker.js
import { imageToSvg } from "img2num";

self.onmessage = async ({ data }) => {
  const { pixels, width, height } = data;
  const { svg } = await imageToSvg({ pixels, width, height });
  self.postMessage(svg);
};

v0.4.2 is what that change unlocked: with no worker plumbing forced into every artifact, each target could finally get a build shaped for its actual environment.

Why did 0.3.0 remove the workers?

Cross-environment compatibility. A hidden worker only made sense in some targets, and it fought any worker architecture you already had. Running on the calling thread works everywhere - Img2Num does the math, and you decide which thread it runs on.

Example apps for every binding​

Talking about build targets is abstract, so the examples got a matching overhaul:

  • console-js is now split into console-js-esm and console-js-cjs, so the import and require export conditions are each exercised by a real consumer (and we fixed a byte-offset bug in the pixel-buffer construction while we were in there).
  • The html-js example was rebuilt as a single shared template compiled into three self-contained variants -

    ESM

     , 

    IIFE

     , and 

    UMD

      - each deployable as plain static files with no build tooling at runtime.
  • The docs site now has an example apps index with a card and representative snippet for every binding: React, browser ESM, IIFE, UMD, Node ESM/CJS - and Python, C++, and C, because Img2Num was never just a JavaScript library.
  • Every JS target is also runnable in your browser right now - the CodeSandbox links in the tabs above are one click from "processed image" with nothing installed.

Each example is intentionally minimal: the shortest path from "empty directory" to "processed image" in your environment of choice. They're also our first line of defense - and this release proved it twice. The React example caught the 0.4.0 browser bug before almost anyone could hit it, and the new Node CJS example caught the CommonJS bug that survived into 0.4.1 the same way. Every entry point now has a real consumer that runs it the way you would.

Getting started​

Using npm
npm install img2num
Using a CDN (the CDN default resolves to the single-file IIFE build)
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/img2num@0.4.2/dist/standalone/img2num.iife.js"></script>

(Pin the version - your future self will thank you.)

What's next​

Purpose-built targets give us a clean baseline for the work we've wanted to do for a while: benchmarking across environments and exploring WebGPU acceleration beyond the current optional Node support. If you hit anything odd with the new builds - an environment we didn't test, an interop edge case - please open an issue so we can fix it for you. Reports from real setups are exactly what a release like this needs.

Thanks for using Img2Num! 🦔🦔

entry.title: We're Expanding the Maintainer Team
entry.summary: Img2Num is expanding its maintainer team across C++, JavaScript, CI/CD, bindings, and documentation. Learn about available roles, maintainer levels, and how to apply.
entry.content:
Img2Num has grown well past the point where one or two people can own it responsibly.

The codebase now spans a performance-critical C++ core, cross-language bindings (Python, JavaScript, C), a WebAssembly build pipeline, CI/CD automation, and a Docusaurus docs site. Keeping all of that high-quality and sustainable requires real ownership — not just occasional PRs.

We're looking for experienced contributors ready to take on scoped, ongoing responsibility.

Architecture Overview​

Img2Num is a layered system. Here's how the pieces fit together:

LayerPathNotes
C++ Corecore/Source of truth for all algorithms
C ABIbindings/c/Stable ABI boundary; feeds the Wasm pipeline
WebAssemblybindings/js/Built via Emscripten from the C ABI
JavaScript packagepackages/js/Safe runtime wrapper over the Wasm module
Python bindingsbindings/py/pybind11 directly on the C++ core
Python packagepackages/py/Exposes the native Python module

Open Maintainer Areas​

CI/CD​

  • GitHub Actions workflows, Docker builds, release pipelines, automated publishing.

C ABI (bindings/c)​

  • Maintain the C ABI over the C++ core. Must stay compatible with external C consumers and the Wasm pipeline.

JavaScript / WebAssembly (bindings/js, packages/js)​

  • Emscripten integration, browser and Node.js compatibility, pnpm workspace tooling, React example app.

Python (bindings/py, packages/py)​

  • pybind11 bindings, uv workspace tooling, console example app.

Docs & DX (docs/, doxygen/)​

  • Docusaurus site, Doxygen integration, tutorials, onboarding experience.

Releases & Packaging​

  • Versioning, tagging, GitHub Releases, npm and Docker Hub publishing.

Testing & Validation​

  • CI test coverage, linting/formatting enforcement, regression testing.

Internal Tooling (scripts/)​

  • Cross-platform CLI utilities, developer automation, local workflow improvements.

Maintainer Tiers​

TierMerge AccessResponsibilities
JuniorNoneReview small PRs, contribute within a defined scope
ScopedWithin their domainOwn a specific area — review, approve, maintain quality
CoreBroadCross-domain architecture, final merge authority, long-term direction

Trust is earned through consistent contributions. Everyone starts scoped.

How to Apply​

Reply to #309 with:

  • Which area(s) you want to own
  • A short summary of relevant experience
  • GitHub profile or projects (optional)

We'll follow up directly.

entry.title: Welcome to Img2Num!
entry.summary: We are excited to launch Img2Num, the interactive app that converts any image into a color-by-number template.
entry.content:
We are excited to launch Img2Num, the interactive app that converts any image into a color-by-number template.

Edit: 20 June 2026

Img2Num is no longer an application for converting images into color-by-number templates. Instead, it is now a library that supports C, C++, Python, and JavaScript.

Try it out online at https://img2num.dev/example-apps/react-js/ and start coloring your favorite images today!

Stay tuned for tutorials, tips, and updates right here on the blog.
